newsitem.title: UK: Labour heading for landslide in UK election - poll.
newsitem.headline: Labour heading for landslide in UK election - poll.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party is heading for a landslide election victory on Thursday that will end 18 years of Conservative rule, opinion pollsters predicted on Tuesday.

But Labour leader Tony Blair, fearing that complacency could torpedo his chances of leading the country into the 21st century, said: "All this talk about landslides -- forget it. We work and struggle for every vote."

Prime Minister John Major, who defied pollsters to score a shock victory in the 1992 election, refused to give up and issued a dramatic warning beneath the famed Tower of Big Ben outside parliament that voters had only three days left to change their minds and save Britain's unity.

"Remember how wrong the polls were before," said Major, who is bidding to give the Conservatives an unprecedented fifth election win in a row against Labour, dragged into the middle ground of British politics by reforming modernist Blair.
But the latest opinion poll in this gruelling six-week campaign made gloomy reading for the Conservatives, riven by mutinies over Britain's role in Europe.
The Gallup poll in the Daily Telegraph showed Labour with a lead of 22 points over the Conservatives, whose two decades in power were launched in 1979 by "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher.
If the poll proved correct on election day, this would translate into a 265-seat majority for Labour in the 659-seat parliament.

Major staged a whirlwind tour of all four corners of Britain on Monday to ram home his point that Labour threatened to break up the United Kingdom with its plans to devolve power to Wales and Scotland and because of its stance in the European Union.
As Big Ben chimed six o'clock, Major said at the end of his round-Britain tour: "The message I would give to you, to the British nation: We have 72 hours to save the Union."

In an election campaign marked by bitter personal attacks, Defence Minister Michael Portillo stepped up the Conservative campaign against Blair as an inexperienced politician who constantly changes his mind to court voters.

Portillo, who could be a leading right-wing contender for Major's job after the election, told the Times newspaper: "Tony Blair's highest aspiration is just to echo what is popular. He is a follower, not a leader."
The Times came out in favour of Eurosceptics of any party who opposed closer integration with the European Union.

That was in sharp contrast to the staunchly pro-Blair stance taken by two other former pro-Conservative papers also owned by the Rupert Murdoch group -- the daily Sun and the weekly News of the World.

The Financial Times, Britain's leading business daily, offered Blair lukewarm support, saying splits in the ruling Conservatives "made it all but impossible for its leaders to implement rational policies towards Europe.
"By default, that opens the door to Mr Tony Blair and Labour. This does not amount to anything like an enthusiastic endorsement," it said.
